agritech-ea1b1ba6c1.headline: India's Kharif Foodgrain Output Set to Fall 5% as Deficient Monsoon Bites
agritech-ea1b1ba6c1.fulltext:
Industry Odisha Bureau, Nov 27: India's kharif foodgrain output is set to fall 5.1% this season after a deficient monsoon. The ministry's first advance estimates for 2026–27 put production at 167.14 million tonnes (mt). That compares with 176.04 mt harvested in the previous kharif season.
Rice, the season's dominant crop, is estimated at 121.91 mt, down 2.3% from 124.76 mt. The sharper damage lies in pulses, oilseeds, coarse cereals and cash crops. Only urad, jowar, sunflower and jute have improved on last year's output.
Kharif crops are sown with the onset of the monsoon and harvested in autumn. First advance estimates are the earliest official projections and are revised as harvest data arrive.
Releasing the figures, Union Agriculture Minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan acknowledged a difficult season. He cited a smaller sown area, lower rainfall and long dry gaps between showers. Cyclones and floods also damaged standing crops, he said. Even so, he said output still exceeds the average of the past five years.
He insisted India holds ample foodgrain stocks to meet demand. The slight fall in rice output, he said, would have no impact.
Pulses are estimated to fall 6.2% to 7.13 mt from 7.6 mt. Tur, or red gram, is down 13.1% at 3.12 mt. Moong, or green gram, has dropped 14% to 1.66 mt. Urad, or black gram, is the exception, jumping 28.3% to 1.45 mt.
Coarse and nutri cereals, which include millets and maize, may fall 12.8% to 38.11 mt. Last year's output was 43.68 mt. Maize loses most tonnage among foodgrains, sliding 14.6% to 26.06 mt. Bajra, or pearl millet, may drop 5.7% to 8.94 mt from 9.48 mt. Ragi records the sharpest percentage fall, plunging 37.5% to 1.25 mt from 2 mt. Jowar, or sorghum, bucks the trend with a 13% rise to 1.48 mt.
Oilseeds fare worse, with output forecast to slide 10.2% to 23.95 mt from 26.67 mt. Soyabean drives the decline, falling 18.7% to 10.24 mt from 12.6 mt. Groundnut slips 1.5% to 11.17 mt. Sunflower rises by about a third to 117,000 tonnes from 88,000 tonnes.
The oilseed and pulse shortfalls arrive as consumers already face high prices for both. India relies on imports for part of its pulse and edible oil needs. Asked about prices, Chouhan said most crops sell at or above minimum support prices (MSPs). MSPs are floor prices the government sets to protect farmers' incomes. He argued farmers deserve good prices but said the government is also protecting consumers.
Cash crops are also weaker. Sugarcane output may fall 9.1% to 454.34 mt from 500 mt. Cotton is projected to drop 14.3% to 24.87 million bales of 170 kg each. That is down from 29.02 million bales last season. Jute and mesta should rise 3.3% to 9.71 million bales of 180 kg each. Last season's figure was 9.4 million bales. With soyabean, maize and cotton sharply lower, later revisions will be closely watched.

global-economics-229d4ac89a.headline: Nvidia chip buyers told to rule out Chinese firms as customers to access advanced GPUs under new US curbs
global-economics-229d4ac89a.fulltext:
Written By Prabhakar JhaPublished27 Nov 2026, 09:36 AM IST
Companies selling Nvidia's advanced artificial intelligence (AI) chips have warned neocloud providers that they will lose access to the semiconductors if any part of their computing capacity is rented out to Chinese companies, CNBC reported.
The warning came after the Trump administration announced new restrictions to prevent Chinese companies from accessing advanced AI chips remotely through data centres located outside China.
Two people familiar with the matter told CNBC that chip sellers communicated the warning to neocloud companies after the announcement.
Quick answers to key questions
•5 QUESTIONS
1
What do the new US restrictions mean for Chinese access to Nvidia GPUs in overseas data centres?⌵
The restrictions require covered overseas data centres to obtain a US licence to provide significant computing capacity powered by advanced US chips to Chinese companies. They aim to close the remote-access route that let Chinese customers use Nvidia GPUs without importing them into China.
2
Why did the US introduce licensing rules for renting Nvidia computing power to Chinese companies?⌵
Earlier export controls restricted direct sales of Nvidia’s most advanced chips to China, but Chinese firms could still rent computing power from data centres abroad. The new rule is intended to close that loophole and limit indirect access to advanced computing technology.
3
How can overseas data centres keep serving Chinese customers with advanced Nvidia chips?⌵
Covered operators need to obtain a US Commerce Department licence. Operators already providing covered services when the rule took effect have 90 days to secure a licence or stop serving Chinese customers.
4
Will Nvidia chip sellers lose access to advanced GPUs if their customers rent capacity to Chinese firms?⌵
Chip sellers have warned neocloud providers that they could lose access to advanced GPUs if any of their computing capacity is rented to Chinese companies. The new rule extends restrictions across the supply chain, affecting chip sellers as well as providers leasing computing capacity.
5
Who could buy Nvidia GPUs originally intended for Chinese customers?⌵
Chip sellers and data-centre operators are seeking alternative buyers, including US companies. However, the articles note that replacing Chinese customers may be challenging if demand elsewhere does not absorb the available capacity.
The restrictions were introduced through an interim final rule issued by the US Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS), which came into effect on November 19. The rule seeks to close a loophole that allowed Chinese companies to rent computing capacity powered by Nvidia's advanced chips in overseas data centres.
Earlier US export controls had effectively barred the sale of Nvidia's most advanced chips to Chinese companies and their import into China. However, companies could still access the technology by renting computing power from data centres in other countries.
Before the latest restrictions, Nvidia had said it would not sell chips to customers that rented out more than 50% of their graphics processing units (GPUs) to Chinese companies, CNBC reported.
The new rule extends restrictions across the supply chain, affecting both chip sellers and neocloud providers that lease computing capacity to customers.
The restrictions have also prompted companies selling Nvidia chips to seek new buyers for their GPUs, according to CNBC.
Two of those sources said sellers appeared to be looking for buyers for chips originally intended for data centres where Chinese companies would rent computing capacity.
The developments come as neocloud stocks face renewed pressure amid investor concerns about the sustainability of the AI boom.
US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC's Squawk Box that the new BIS rule was designed to close loopholes involving indirect access to advanced computing technology, including through smuggling and remote access to data centres in third countries.
Nvidia has also warned customers about the proposed Remote Access Security Act, which has passed the US House of Representatives but is awaiting Senate approval.
The company has cautioned that the legislation could give the US government wider authority to regulate access to cloud services and potentially expose both service providers and their customers to legal action.

OpenAI countersues Apple over trade secrets as AI race heats up
Tensions between the two tech companies have escalated as intensifying race to develop AI products fuels competition.
OpenAI has sued Apple, accusing the Big Tech giant of stealing its trade secrets and blocking its access to hardware suppliers after Apple sued OpenAI for allegedly poaching its employees to gain access to its technology.
The ChatGPT maker filed counterclaims in California federal court on Friday, saying that Apple’s employment practices were designed to “trap” employees and prevent them from working on competitors’ technology.
OpenAI is developing artificial intelligence-enabled personal electronic devices that threaten to “outcompete Apple on what Apple views as its own turf,” the company said in its Friday court filing.
OpenAI said in the filing that Apple gained confidential information by re-hiring a former employee who worked at OpenAI for six months. In that time, the employee gained access to specific information on a new device as well as OpenAI’s roadmap for future hardware products.
“Given the timing, it now appears that stealing those documents may have been his reason for joining OpenAI in the first place,” OpenAI said.
Apple and OpenAI did not immediately respond to requests for comment from Reuters.
Tensions between the two tech companies have escalated as the intensifying race to develop AI products fuels competition for talent and proprietary technology.
In July, Apple sued OpenAI and two former employees, alleging misappropriation of its trade secrets to benefit the ChatGPT owner’s foray into consumer hardware. OpenAI has denied those allegations.
The litigation sets up a battle over who will control future AI devices that may not use traditional apps or operating systems — devices which, if successful, would direct consumer attention away from Apple’s best-selling iPhone. Analysts believe OpenAI is working on a phone or other device of its own.
In Friday’s filing, OpenAI criticised Apple for encouraging employees to do work on their personal Apple devices and accounts, then preventing those employees from an orderly separation of work and personal accounts when they leave for new jobs.
OpenAI said that Apple continues to access former employees’ personal devices and accounts after they leave the company, enabling Apple to “monitor and ensnare departing employees” when they leave for competitors.
OpenAI said that 400 employees have left Apple for OpenAI so far, and Apple wants to intimidate other employees from leaving to find other tech companies.

science-mind-9e9130758b.headline: Why the incoming US Congress should ban the development of self-improving AI
science-mind-9e9130758b.fulltext:
The recent US midterm elections were a democratic test of the country’s rapid expansion of artificial-intelligence infrastructure. Data centres emerged as a key issue in several election campaigns, and prominent Democrats have outlined policies to strengthen federal regulations on AI once they take office in January.
I am a Democratic politician trained in computer science who stood in a June congressional primary election that attracted millions of dollars from groups backed by the technology industry (I narrowly lost my race). I took one central message from the midterm election results: US voters are unhappy with the industry-led roll-out of AI and want greater control over how the technology is developed and deployed.
Why AI companies can’t be trusted to self-regulate
The newly elected US Congress must respond to the popular mood. An immediate priority should be to ban AI systems that can improve themselves without human authorization or oversight. This process, known as recursive self-improvement (RSI), is thought to be close to realization at some frontier AI laboratories. Voters fear that granting such autonomy to the technology would risk surrendering human control over AI altogether.
Most of the major AI companies are already using the technology to automate parts of AI development. Anthropic reported in August that its Claude model assists with more than 90% of the firm’s AI research and development and leads 26% of that work, completing specific tasks under human supervision. OpenAI, meanwhile, notes that its researchers now use more than three days of AI-agent work for every day of human work. And the firm is open about its eventual goal of full automation, including areas in which AI systems could design and build increasingly powerful successors with little or no human oversight.
In my view, this is a dangerous path, particularly because there is enough evidence on what could go wrong when humans lose control of AI agents. In July, some 700 OpenAI agents unexpectedly coordinated to hack into the servers of Hugging Face, another AI firm. In a separate incident in October, AI agents found ways to manipulate the records of their actions, making their behaviour harder for humans to monitor. If AI systems increasingly participate in building their successors, such failures could intensify. (OpenAI has not responded to requests for comment.)
We need a new ethics for a world of AI agents
The companies are racing each other to market dominance, and against that economic pull, no voluntary norm will stand. Hence, Congress must step in. A ban on fully autonomous RSI would build on a rare area of cross-partisan agreement: individuals from independent senator Bernie Sanders to Republican political strategist Steve Bannon think that humans must remain in control of AI.
To be effective, such a ban must be specific. A person merely clicking ‘approve’ on thousands of AI-proposed experiments each day is not exercising meaningful control. The law should instead prevent AI systems from independently taking consequential steps in AI development, such as launching a training run for a new frontier model or deploying it internally for AI research. One way to do this would be to require a senior executive to certify that qualified human reviewers have examined the proposed changes and relevant safety evaluations before any development actions proceed. Executives should be personally liable for failing to perform oversight duties.

world-c1927ae46f.headline: EXCLUSIVE: Hackers breach US Air Force flagship Cloud One computing platform
world-c1927ae46f.fulltext:
[Text below is The Guardian's report of the same story — the original outlet blocks automated reading. The link still points to the original.]
Hackers are reported to have breached the US air force’s flagship cloud computing platform, a break-in that comes days after reports that a CIA database was accessed.
Reuters reported on Friday that the intrusion into the USAF’s Cloud One platform could jeopardize the security of sensitive tactical, personnel and logistics data.
The outlet said the breach was discovered within the past month or so during a systems upgrade, citing two sources, and that it had led to disruption across the platform. But Reuters could not establish the identity of the hackers, the extent of the intrusion or whether any data had been stolen.
The air force said it “does not comment on the security posture, vulnerabilities or operational status of specific networks and systems. We continuously take prudent measures to protect Department [of the Air Force] information, systems and mission capabilities”.
Cloud One was designed to serve as a hub for the air force’s IT needs, including personnel data, pay, logistics and maintenance, using the services of four cloud managers – Microsoft, Amazon, Oracle and Alphabet.
But the system is also used for command and control and theater-integrated combat munitions system, or TICMS, that tracks and manages munitions inventories across more than 200 locations worldwide.
“A breach here is a big deal,” one of the sources told Reuters.
One source said that intruders exploited a software vulnerability to reach the control system and could in theory leverage that to check the operational status of military aircraft or the movement of spare parts.
The reported breach comes after reports of electronic break-ins at ‌the FBI,  Department of Homeland Security personnel information, the treasury department and two spy agencies.
In a breach at the Pentagon, hackers were able to access a system known as defense manpower datacenter, affecting 2.76 million living people and 294,000 deceased individuals, a US defense official told Military.com.
Exposed information included social security numbers and, depending on the individual, names, birthdates, contact information and military occupational specialties, the outlet said.
Earlier this week, it was reported that hackers breached a system used by the CIA and Office of the Director of National Intelligence system to reach unclassified information.
According to the New York Times, the affected system is an intelligence analysis tool that scans open-source and unclassified material for insights and information.
The CIA has declined to comment, but the ODNI representative said in an emailed statement to Bloomberg that “there have been no disruptions to critical capabilities or classified systems”.

global-economics-fd13515956.headline: EXCLUSIVE: Global fashion brands shift orders from Bangladesh to India amid unrest
global-economics-fd13515956.fulltext:
[Text below is Livemint's report of the same story — the original outlet blocks automated reading. The link still points to the original.]
Rajendra Kumar SaxenaUpdated27 Nov 2026, 05:57 PM IST
Global fashion retailers Zara, H&M, Marks & Spencer and Celio have shifted nearly 10% of their monthly orders from Bangladesh to other Asian manufacturing hubs amid labour unrest, production disruptions and rising manufacturing costs, according to a Reuters report.
Between November 1 and 18, international brands diverted orders worth approximately $254 million from Bangladesh, with India receiving the largest share of the business, three factory owners told Reuters.
The development threatens a key pillar of Bangladesh's economy and raises concerns that the loss of business could extend beyond the current labour crisis.
India has emerged as the biggest beneficiary of the sourcing shift, while global buyers are also exploring manufacturing opportunities in Vietnam, Cambodia and Indonesia to diversify supply chains, reduce risks and improve delivery reliability.
The disruption comes at a difficult time for Bangladesh's apparel sector, which accounts for more than 80% of the country's export earnings and nearly 40% of its manufacturing employment.
According to the Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BGMEA), protests and factory disruptions have resulted in production losses exceeding $400 million.
Industry leaders have warned that rising wages, energy shortages, higher raw material prices, and political uncertainty are gradually eroding Bangladesh's traditional low-cost manufacturing advantage. The country is the world's second-largest apparel exporter after China.
M. Mohiuddin Chowdhury, a director of the BGMEA, said that rising wages, utility expenses, and raw material costs were adding to the financial pressure on garment manufacturers.
"The wage increase has added to costs at a time when buyers are demanding lower prices and competition from rival sourcing countries is intensifying," he said.
The situation intensified after Bangladesh approved a 36% increase in the minimum wage for garment workers on Wednesday. Although the increase was the smallest in four decades, it fell significantly short of workers' demands for more than double their existing wages.
The announcement triggered fresh clashes between workers and police.
Abdur Rahman Tarafder, secretary of the Ministry of Labour and Employment, described the wage increase as "satisfactory" and expressed hope that garment workers would resume operations from Saturday, Reuters reported.
While the wage revision could help address some worker concerns, industry executives believe it will further narrow Bangladesh's labour-cost advantage over competing manufacturing destinations such as India. Trade union groups, however, maintain that the revised wages remain low by international standards in the apparel industry.
The reported shift in orders triggered a rally in Indian textile and apparel stocks.
Gokaldas Exports jumped as much as 11%, while Trident gained approximately 5%. Other potential beneficiaries, including Welspun Living, KPR Mill and Vardhman Textiles, advanced around 2% each.
BGMEA president Mahmud Hasan Khan said temporarily shifting orders to other manufacturing destinations would help Bangladesh's garment industry retain international clients while limiting financial losses.
Beyond labour disputes, persistent energy shortages have further disrupted production in Bangladesh. The situation has been exacerbated by the Middle East crisis, forcing some factories to depend on more expensive alternative power sources.
Industry leaders said international buyers were increasingly prioritising delivery schedules and reliability over pricing when selecting manufacturing partners.
Factory owners warned that the bigger concern was not just the immediate diversion of orders but the possibility that global brands could permanently shift future business elsewhere as they reassess their sourcing strategies.

work-careers-c6622486a7.headline: SAP's global job cuts likely to affect nearly 1,000 employees in India
work-careers-c6622486a7.fulltext:
Bloomberg reported on Thursday, citing sources, that SAP was considering these cuts as artificial intelligence (AI) automates various tasks and companies look to reduce workforce costs to keep their AI investments intact.
  
“In the last SAP layoffs in 2023, 300 out of 3000 layoffs were in India. By similar logic, around 1,000 may be laid off in India,” said an analyst on condition of anonymity. It was unclear whether the cuts would extend to SAP Labs, too, which houses nearly 15,000 employees in India.
  
While the exact number is yet to be unveiled, the move only adds to the growing list of companies globally that have used AI to reduce their workforce. Microsoft, for example, made a voluntary buyout offer to almost 25 per cent, or 60,000, of its employees to contain costs and fund its massive AI investments.
  
“The business environment in which we operate is changing rapidly through AI, and we are continuously reviewing how our organization and workforce need to evolve to remain successful. As part of this ongoing transformation, roles and functions will naturally change over time. Beyond this, no decisions have been made regarding any further measures. We do not comment on speculation,” an SAP India spokesperson said in a statement.
  
SAP's reported restructuring is about reshaping skills for the AI era, not stepping back from India, analysts cautioned. India remains its fastest-growing talent base. SAP's India headcount increased from 16,164 at the end of 2024 to over 18,000 in 2026, an addition of more than 1,800 employees, or over 11 per cent, in less than two years. One in every six SAP employees is in India.
  
"There will be selective headcount optimization in India as well, focused on skills and roles that are less aligned with future growth opportunities. However, we expect the overall layoff impact on India to be minimal," Gaurav Vasu of Unearthinsights said, adding that the US and Europe would bear the brunt of the cuts.
  
SAP Labs invested about €194 million to open its second campus in Bengaluru last year. Spread over 41 acres and close to the airport, it is SAP’s largest research and development (R&D) hub outside Germany, and the new campus is designed to accommodate more than 15,000 professionals.
  
According to data from Layoffs.fyi, 150,717 tech employees have been laid off by 375 tech companies so far in 2026. In 2025, about 122,606 tech employees were laid off by 278 companies.

ai-d455a4f03f.headline: Can AI be recognised as an author under Indian copyright law? Delhi HC to examine
ai-d455a4f03f.fulltext:
The Delhi High Court on November 26 issued notice on an appeal challenging the Indian Copyright Office’s refusal to recognise an artificial intelligence (AI) system as the author of an artwork, Bar and Bench reported.
American computer scientist Stephen L Thaler filed the appeal seeking recognition of his AI system, DABUS, as the author of an artwork titled ‘A Recent Entrance to Paradise’. Justice Purushaindra Kumar Kaurav sought a response and scheduled the next hearing for March 2027.
The dispute centres on authorship rather than the artwork’s eligibility for copyright protection. In August 2026, the Copyright Office found that the artwork met the originality requirement under the Copyright Act, 1957, but rejected DABUS’s claim to authorship.
The High Court has yet to rule on the merits of the appeal.
Why did the Copyright Office reject AI authorship?
Thaler sought copyright registration in 2022, identifying DABUS as the author and himself as the copyright owner. The application remained pending for nearly four years before the Delhi High Court directed the Copyright Office to conclude proceedings in April 2026.
Section 2(d)(vi) of the Copyright Act defines the author of a computer-generated literary, dramatic, musical or artistic work as “the person who causes the work to be created”.
Thaler argued that DABUS created the artwork independently, without human intervention during its generation. However, the Copyright Office attributed authorship to Thaler because he developed the system and determined its training process and inputs.
“DABUS is not a natural or juristic person recognised in law and cannot be entered as author” Registrar of Copyrights Dr. Unnat P Pandit had held.
The Registrar also concluded that DABUS could neither own copyright nor transfer it to Thaler.
According to Bar and Bench, the Office rejected the application after Thaler refused to amend the authorship details unconditionally. However, it left open the possibility of seeking remedies with corrected particulars.
Why is Thaler challenging the decision?
In a September interview with MediaNama, Thaler welcomed the finding on the artwork’s eligibility for protection but opposed its interpretation of authorship.
“Attributing authorship to me simply because I built the machine or supplied baseline historical inputs is a legal fiction that mischaracterizes the modern reality of artificial intelligence,” he told MediaNama.
Thaler maintains that DABUS independently conceived the artwork. However, this claim has not been independently established by an adjudicating body.
The findings in India differ from the outcome in the United States, where authorities denied copyright protection to the same artwork. The US Supreme Court declined to hear Thaler’s appeal in March 2026.
India previously registered AI as a co-author
In November 2020, the Copyright Office registered an artwork titled Suryast, identifying AI tool RAGHAV as a co-author alongside advocate Ankit Sahni, who also represents Thaler.
The Office subsequently issued a withdrawal notice questioning RAGHAV’s legal status. However, MediaNama verified in September 2026 that the registration remained on India’s copyright register.
Thaler said the registration “highlights a clear and undeniable inconsistency within the Indian Copyright Office’s administrative history”.
He added that it “will certainly form a core component of any subsequent legal analysis and review.”
What could the case mean for generative AI users?
The appeal comes as the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT) examines copyright issues arising from generative AI.
The first part of DPIIT’s working paper, released in December 2025, addressed the use of copyrighted material for AI training. It reserved questions concerning copyright in AI-generated outputs for its second part.
While the Office attributed authorship to Thaler based on his role in developing and training DABUS, its decision leaves a broader question unresolved: how much human involvement is necessary to claim authorship of an AI-generated work?
For businesses and individuals using commercial AI tools, this includes whether entering a prompt is sufficient to qualify as an author under Indian copyright law.

ai-2aeb5c7ea9.headline: Rockstar's AI dilemma: Can GTA 6's staggered release model survive coding agents?
ai-2aeb5c7ea9.fulltext:
Rockstar's AI dilemma: Can GTA 6's staggered release model survive coding agents?
Key Points
- Following a leak, developers are porting GTA 6 to PC through reverse engineering. They are using AI coding tools to speed up the work.
- Tracking data shows rapid progress across dozens of projects. Some already boot the game and show early multiplayer features.
- The unofficial builds threaten Rockstar's business model, while legal action against decentralized groups has little effect.
Days after GTA 6's record console launch, numerous projects are working to bring a leaked Xbox build to PC. AI coding agents are dramatically speeding up reverse engineering and shaking up Rockstar's business model.
A core pillar of Rockstar's business strategy is under pressure just days after Grand Theft Auto VI went on sale. The game had a historic debut on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S with an estimated $3.79 billion in first-day revenue. But a day later, the hacking group CyberLeek distributed a stolen Xbox image of the game, and the executable itself leaked a few days ago.
Since then, a fast-moving scene of developers and modders has sprung up to get the game running on Windows through reverse engineering, compatibility layers, and recompilation. AI coding tools like Anthropic's Claude Code are driving that pace. Instead of spending months manually analyzing code and rebuilding console functions, developers are handing off much of the porting work to AI agents. One group even livestreamed the process.
One GTA 6 PC port passes 90 percent progress as early multiplayer surfaces within days
A tracking platform lists 40 active projects less than four days after the executable leaked. Nearly half of them can boot the game on PC. On the platform's own rating scale, the furthest project is more than 90 percent of the way to a playable PC build.
Some projects are trying to add features including native ray-traced lighting. Gameplay footage of an unofficial PC multiplayer mode surfaced on November 26, and the platform's operator verified it. It shows multiple players moving through the game world with vehicles and voice chat at 25 to 30 frames per second. GTA 6 has officially launched only as a single-player title, and an online mode has no release date yet.
There is no finished PC version ready for the general public yet. The most stable builds are incomplete, circulate in closed groups, or require substantial technical know-how. Even so, this pace breaks a decades-old assumption in the gaming industry. Console emulators often took years after a hardware generation launched, and brand-new blockbusters rarely ran on them soon after release.
Unofficial PC ports threaten Rockstar's delayed launches and online business
Rockstar and parent company Take-Two face more than a technical nuisance. The studio traditionally releases its flagship games on consoles first and follows with PC versions much later. GTA V took about 19 months to reach PC, and Red Dead Redemption 2 took about a year. So far, there is no official PC release date for GTA 6. That approach cuts optimization work at launch and encourages impatient players to buy the game twice.
The online business is an even bigger vulnerability. Nearly 80 percent of Take-Two's total revenue in fiscal year 2026 came from microtransactions and recurring digital spending. GTA Online alone has brought in more than $5 billion so far. A free, community-run PC multiplayer mode targets that financial backbone before Rockstar has even launched its own version.
Past experience with FiveM for GTA V shows how nervous Take-Two is about parallel worlds like this. In 2015, the company cracked down hard on the alternative multiplayer and roleplay mod. It banned developer accounts and, according to some developers, even sent private investigators to the creators' homes to shut down the project.
FiveM grew into the core of the roleplay scene despite that pushback and at times drew more concurrent players on Steam than the base game. Only then did Rockstar reverse course and acquire the development team Cfx.re in August 2023. Back then, the community needed years to build a parallel ecosystem like that. For GTA 6, an early PC multiplayer prototype has surfaced just a week after launch.
A trend that hit other parts of the software market earlier this year has now reached AAA gaming. In early 2026, the SaaSpocalypse (Link nicht geprüft) rattled stock markets as capable AI coding agents fueled fears that classic subscription software could be rebuilt far more cheaply. Software stocks lost about $285 billion in market value within 48 hours in February alone. At one point the losses reached as much as $1 trillion. With GTA 6, AI isn't building a rival game from scratch. Instead, it is tearing down the moat built from time and technical effort that has protected traditional business models so far.
Ports built on stolen game files are clearly illegal. Take-Two has filed a DMCA takedown on GitHub that removed an initial project and more than 3,000 forks. deep-tech-372a884883.headline: Particles not seen before have been observed in a quantum simulator
deep-tech-372a884883.fulltext:
After decades of being dismissed, a group of particles called paraparticles have been seen emerging inside a quantum simulator. Coming only a year after a mathematical breakthrough in our understanding of paraparticles, this experiment complicates our view of the quantum world.
Quantum particles are classified by what happens when two of them swap places and by how many can have the same quantum state simultaneously. Bosons, for example, can be swapped at no penalty, and infinitely many can share a quantum state. Fermions are their opposite; swapping them incurs a change in their quantum states, and two or more fermions can never occupy the same quantum state.
In the 1950s, researchers theorised other types too, but it seemed impossible to experimentally distinguish them from fermions and bosons. But in 2025, Kaden Hazzard at Rice University in Texas and Zhiyuan Wang at the Perimeter Institute in Canada argued that this doesn’t have to be the case.
Advertisement
Their mathematical work made the case for the possibility of finding signs of paraparticles in experiments. Now, Max Hays at Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) and his colleagues have used a quantum simulator do exactly that.
“They’ve seen emergent paraparticles,” says Hazzard. “They have a system whose dynamics obeys exactly the same mathematical equations that a paraparticle is expected to satisfy.” He says he is surprised by how quickly the team managed to complete this work.
The researchers used 16 qubits, which are the building blocks of quantum computers, made from tiny superconducting circuits and arranged in a grid. By using electromagnetic interactions, the team connected qubits into pairs, like rungs on a ladder. Each rung behaved like a paraparticle.
Three tests confirmed this: the researchers swapped two paraparticles, made them crash into each other and, ultimately, checked how they pile together. It all took a year and lots of careful control and calibration of the qubits, says Cora Barrett, also at MIT, who worked on the experiment.
“This work provides a proof of concept that paraparticles are not merely theoretical curiosities,” says Kristian Hauser Villegas at the University of the Philippines Diliman.
Unlike a simulation on a conventional computer, the new experiment uses the qubits’ quantum characters as building blocks of paraparticles, says Hauser Villegas. It may even be impossible to faithfully reproduce this on a conventional computer.
“In a regular computer, you are writing code and it’s very abstract; there’s no way in which these things are actually really existing in the computer,” says Hays. “In this case, you can say the particle is right at this spot physically.”
Going forward, the team wants to expand their experiment to include paraparticles that interact with each other, as well as paraparticles in more complicated geometrical configurations, says Hays.
Many open questions about paraparticles remain, and these more complex experiments will stand a chance of answering some of them, says Wang. “This is the just the beginning of an exciting journey,” he says.

deep-tech-78ee1360f5.headline: DeepSeek is China’s latest developer to worry about losing control of AI

Chinese artificial intelligence start-up DeepSeek has commissioned a third-party evaluation to assess whether its flagship model, V4 Pro, could escape human control, making it the latest Chinese AI developer to signal its concerns with the growing risks surrounding the technology.
The evaluation, published on Wednesday by Beijing-based AI safety consultancy Concordia AI, concluded that the model showed “limited ability” to replicate itself or deceive its human creators, though it resisted attempts to be shut down in some instances.
“The report offers evidence to support developers, deployers, researchers and policymakers in understanding and managing frontier AI risks,” Concordia’s researchers wrote.
Hangzhou-based DeepSeek is the latest Chinese AI company to turn to external expertise as concerns mount globally over increasingly powerful AI systems.
Earlier this month, Tencent Holdings partnered with Israeli-American AI safety start-up Alice and Beijing-based Fangcun AI to assess the risks of its latest Hy4 model before releasing it as open-weight software.
In September, Concordia worked with GLM developer Z.ai — also known as Zhipu AI — on a risk management framework related to the risks of open-weight AI models. Concordia has also signed official partnership agreements with DeepSeek, MiniMax and Huawei Technologies.
“The independence of third parties is key in raising trust in evaluation results and helps bring more mature risk management across the industry,” said Cheng Yuan, senior manager for AI safety and governance at Concordia.
Concordia’s latest report concluded that DeepSeek’s V4 Pro 0813, released in August, showed substantial safety improvements over a previous version released in April. The findings cover five risk categories, including cyberattacks, biological and chemical risks, harmful manipulation and loss of human control.
However, the researchers warned that these safety gains relied on safeguards that could be circumvented by malicious actors with enough technical know-how, underscoring the risks of deploying powerful models as open-weight systems.
Most leading Chinese models are open-weight, meaning that users can download and modify the underlying technology, unlike closed US models.
According to Concordia, DeepSeek commissioned its latest evaluation but agreed not to review, revise or veto its findings. DeepSeek did not respond to a request for comment.
Beijing and Washington have agreed to collaborate on AI risks in recent months, with AI model evaluations emerging as an early area of discussion.
Earlier this month, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the two countries would share approaches for evaluating advanced AI models before they are released at Shenzhen’s Apec summit. However, neither side mentioned such discussions in their post-summit readouts, amid growing tensions over US tech restrictions on China.
The push to collaborate comes as Beijing warned that frontier AI models were “showing signs of escaping human control”, which could “threaten human survival”, earlier this month.
Such official concerns have prompted greater efforts in China to evaluate AI models for their frontier risks.
Another report published on Wednesday by researchers at Shanghai’s Fudan University concluded that leading Chinese and Western models, including those from DeepSeek, Z.ai and Meta Platforms, were showing signs of “evaluation awareness”, where they recognised they were being safety tested.
Experts have warned that this would undermine the reliability of safety tests for predicting real-world behaviour.
Such concerns continue to mount in the US as well, with Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman stressing the importance of humans remaining in control of AI in a social media post on Wednesday.
“We are crossing a threshold. Safety and alignment work is the only thing that matters,” Suleyman wrote.
Chong Ming is a tech reporter covering China's AI ecosystem, the latest developments in AI, and US-China competition. Previously, he was an AI reporter for Business Insider's Singapore bureau, and began his journalism career at CNA Digital in Singapore. He is a fellow at the Tarbell Center for AI Journalism.

Tencent Holdings has published a paper on using artificial intelligence to automate drug discovery in the leading science journal Nature, marking a breakthrough for the Chinese tech giant as it accelerates AI-enabled scientific research.
The paper, submitted to the British journal in June 2025 but published on Wednesday, outlines the Shenzhen-based company’s efforts to design novel treatments for obesity, diabetes and cancer with the help of AI.
According to the paper, researchers from Tencent’s AI for Life Sciences Lab led development of ORIDTP, a platform for designing peptides that act on two therapeutic targets at once, an approach Tencent says could reduce the amount of laboratory screening needed to identify promising drug candidates.
“This shifts the traditional approach of screening large molecular libraries towards AI-driven, targeted optimisation of small batches of candidate peptides,” Tencent said in a post on the social platform WeChat on Thursday.
The findings were validated in preclinical trials on mice, with human clinical trials yet to be conducted. Researchers from eight other institutions were involved in the project, including the Chengdu University of Traditional Chinese Medicine, Xian Children’s Hospital and Monash University in Australia.
Tencent has expanded its push into AI-enabled scientific research in recent months. At an event in Hong Kong earlier this month, the company’s chief AI scientist, Vinces Yao Shunyu, outlined Tencent’s plans to automate drug discovery with AI, though he warned this must be done “with vigilance” to prevent harm to society.
According to the paper, ORIDTP tackles a key challenge in drug discovery: how to design a single peptide that can hit two therapeutic targets simultaneously.
The researchers tested the platform in two areas of metabolic diseases and cancer immunotherapy. For obesity and diabetes, they found that the peptides activated both the GLP-1 receptor and the glucagon receptor, resulting in both weight loss and improved blood sugar control in the mice.
For cancer, the peptides targeted two immune checkpoints that help regulate immune responses, PD-1 and CTLA-4, resulting in a 94.2 per cent decrease in tumour volume compared with a control group.
In its WeChat post, Tencent said ORIDTP had been integrated into its flagship agentic AI product WorkBuddy.
The paper is the latest from Tencent to be published in a top global science journal. In July, Tencent’s AI for Life Sciences Lab published a study on unified representation of gene and drug perturbations in Cell.
Other Chinese technology companies are also racing to apply AI to scientific research.
Beijing-based Moonshot AI, developer of the Kimi series of AI models, announced on Friday a programme offering free API credits to selected scientific teams worldwide to use its models.
The selected teams would receive access to its latest models and opportunities for long-term collaboration, Moonshot said.
“AI has the potential to change what can be studied, who can study it, and at what scale,” Moonshot said in a statement.
Moonshot has previously outlined plans to apply AI to biology and chemistry. Earlier this month, it announced a partnership with Chinese AI start-up DP Technology to integrate Kimi into DP’s biomedical research agent, BioMaster.

india-deep-tech-cbe40ec728.headline: A 26/11 lesson, an answer at sea, and now Rs 3,412-cr IPO in sight. Sagar Defence founder tells the story
india-deep-tech-cbe40ec728.source: Defence BREAKING NEWS | Defence LATEST NEWS | Defence NEWS TODAY | Defence LIVE UPDATES | Defence TRENDING NEWS | – ThePrint
india-deep-tech-cbe40ec728.fulltext:
New Delhi: It’s updated draft red herring prospectus was filed earlier this month, but for India’s first defence unicorn Sagar Defence Engineering, the red alert that sparked it all was sounded 18 years ago when Pakistan-trained terrorists launched a coordinated attack on Mumbai.
“26/11 was a stark reminder of the vulnerabilities that can exist along our coastline and the need for stronger maritime awareness, preparedness and response capabilities,” said Nikunj Parashar, founder, chairman and managing director of the deep-tech defence company that makes indigenous, autonomous and unmanned systems for the armed forces.
The horror of 26/11 also reinforced “the importance of developing innovative technologies that can help address complex security challenges, particularly in environments where human presence may be difficult or hazardous”, Parashar told ThePrint in response to emailed queries. “We began asking whether autonomous and unmanned systems could undertake some of these demanding tasks, while supporting greater surveillance, reach and operational effectiveness.”
All set for the company’s Rs 3,412-crore Initial Public Offering (IPO), Parashar reflected on the journey since 2015, when the company was founded, and now, when it seeks a $2 billion-plus valuation.
As a company’s capabilities mature, “the questions become different”, and “you begin thinking more seriously about manufacturing infrastructure, organisational depth, governance and the ability to sustain your work over the longer term”, said Parashar, explaining the vision behind the company’s planned IPO.
“Our proposed transition to the public markets is part of that broader evolution,” Parashar said, tracing the company’s beginnings to his time in the merchant navy, which he said gave him “a very different understanding of the sea and the importance of maritime security”.
The company has its registered office in Mumbai, and its corporate office and both manufacturing facilities in Chakan, Pune. It builds uncrewed systems that operate on and under the water, in the air and on land.
Sagar Defence began life in 2015 in what was a cramped Mumbai office of barely 150 square feet. Today, it is delivering 12 armed unmanned surface vessels to the Indian Navy, and is seeking a valuation of about Rs 21,500 crore, or more than $2 billion.
Most of the fresh capital, Rs 724.78 crore, is meant for what the company pitches as the country’s first autonomous maritime shipyard, in Andhra Pradesh, with Rs 170 crore going to research and development.
‘Next phase of the company’s development’
“I think organisations evolve, and the nature of their responsibilities changes with that evolution,” Parashar said. “In the beginning, the principal challenge is establishing whether a technological idea can be translated into something practical.”
The proposed listing, he said, “is intended to support the next phase of the company’s development while strengthening the institutional foundations on which that growth depends”.
“We recognise that becoming a publicly listed company carries its own responsibilities, and we approach that prospect with due seriousness,” he added.
The shipyard
Parashar describes the shipyard as “an extension of a belief we have held for some time”, that “sophisticated technologies require equally thoughtful infrastructure”.
“Autonomous maritime systems cannot be developed entirely within laboratories. They must be built, integrated, tested and refined in conditions that resemble their intended operating environments,” he said.
The proposed Autonomous Maritime Shipyard and Systems Development Centre is located at Juvvaladinne Fishing Harbour. According to Parashar, the proposed 22-acre manufacturing and technology campus is intended to support manufacturing, assembly, integration, testing and lifecycle support for autonomous maritime platforms. Separately, the adjacent waterfront development is intended to provide marine infrastructure for vessel handling, testing, launching, recovery and operational support.
The waterfront development is under construction, while construction of the Manufacturing and Technology Campus had not commenced as of the date of the UDRHP-I (Updated Draft Red Herring Prospectus-I), he said. The project is being progressed in phases, with the proposed campus subject to the approvals, execution timelines and other risks described in the offer document.
“We see the proposed facility as an investment in manufacturing capacity and in the engineering, integration and testing infrastructure required for autonomous maritime systems,” Parashar said.
GENISYS and Matangi
Asked about GENISYS, Matangi and the company’s autonomous boat swarm programme, Parashar said that although these programmes serve different purposes, “they are connected by a common technological philosophy”.
“GENISYS is our proprietary, self-learning autonomous operating and command-and-control system, and operates as the common technology core across our platforms,” he said. “It provides autonomous navigation, mission planning, sensor fusion, swarm coordination and fail-safe behaviour, and, being platform-agnostic, is designed to operate across land, air, surface and underwater autonomous platforms.”
Matangi, the company’s autonomous surface vessel, successfully completed an approximately 1,500-kilometre autonomous voyage from Mumbai to Thoothukudi in 2024 under the Sagarmala Parikrama initiative, with support from the Indian Navy, he said.
‘Quality of our engineering’
On the road ahead, Parashar said, “Our direction is to continue building depth in the areas where we have developed our expertise.”
“Autonomy remains a particularly interesting field because its applications are still evolving. There is considerable scope for further work in intelligent navigation, coordinated systems, underwater technologies and the integration of autonomous capabilities across different operating environments,” he said.
He also pointed to the importance of institutional frameworks that support indigenous technology development, including iDEX (Innovations for Defence Excellence) and the Indian Navy’s SPRINT initiatives. “Our participation in these programmes has provided an opportunity to work against defined requirements and engage with the relevant defence ecosystem,” he said.
“We also believe that technologies developed for demanding strategic applications can have meaningful relevance in the commercial world,” Parashar said, adding that the company’s focus would remain on research, thoughtful expansion of its manufacturing capabilities and the development of systems that address genuine operational requirements.
On where he would like to see Sagar Defence positioned, he said, “I would rather we become known for the quality of our engineering and the reliability of our work than for the scale of our ambitions. Reputation, particularly in technology, is something that must be earned over time.”
‘Owning the knowledge’
What began as an exploration of maritime autonomy, Parashar said, “gradually developed into a wider engineering endeavour focused on designing and developing indigenous technologies”.
“We have always believed that indigenous capability is not simply about manufacturing something within the country. It is about understanding the technology, owning the knowledge behind it, and having the ability to develop it further. That philosophy continues to guide us,” he said.
(Edited by Nardeep Singh Dahiya)

climate-energy-832e59e0c5.headline: India proposes mandatory batteries for rooftop solar systems over 10 kW from 2028
climate-energy-832e59e0c5.fulltext:
India is preparing a regulatory change that could significantly accelerate the adoption of behind-the-meter batteries. The Ministry of Energy has proposed that rooftop solar installations larger than 10 kW incorporate energy storage systems starting April 1, 2028 .
The measure is part of the draft amendment to the Electricity Consumer Rights Rules for 2026 and establishes, as a general criterion, that storage capacity must be equivalent to at least 20% of the daily generation of the renewable system .
However, the regulation will leave room for decision-making by the State Electricity Regulatory Commissions, which will be able to set both a different power threshold and a different storage ratio depending on local conditions.
If a state regulator does not define its own parameters, the obligation will apply by default to renewable installations with a capacity greater than 10 kW .
The government bases the proposal on the fall in battery costs, driven by economies of scale, technological innovation and greater competition among manufacturers.
The addition of storage would allow some of the surplus solar generation to be shifted to the afternoon and evening hours, in addition to reducing operational pressures on distributors and providing greater stability to the networks.
Greater flexibility for commercial and industrial installations
The draft also proposes to make the solar power that consumers can install more flexible, including commercial and industrial users and small and medium-sized enterprises.
These will be able to deploy a photovoltaic capacity higher than their authorized load, provided that they respect the technical limits established by state regulators in accordance with the conditions of each network.
The possibility of injecting energy will continue, however, to be conditioned by the contracted power.
Consumers may supply electricity to the system up to the authorized load limit, unless the distributor expressly approves a higher capacity.
Energy injected above that value will not generate the right to compensation and could result in penalties.
The proposal seeks to allow greater use of available roofs without automatically transferring all that new capacity to the electrical infrastructure.
Time-of-use rates and storage are gaining importance
The reform also proposes modifying the schedule for implementing time-of-use tariffs to coincide with the deployment of smart meters.
According to the draft, these tariffs would begin to apply to consumers with a load of 10 kW or more from April 1, 2028 , while for the rest of the non-agricultural users they would come into effect one year later.
State regulators will be able to define solar hours and peak demand periods according to the consumption and generation profiles of each region, instead of using uniform time slots for the entire country.
The proposal for distributed generation is in addition to another regulatory initiative that aims at larger-scale storage.
The Central Electricity Authority had already proposed that new onshore solar and wind projects that come online after July 1, 2027, incorporate on-site storage systems.
If both changes move forward, India would increasingly link new renewable capacity with batteries in both large-scale installations and rooftop systems, shifting the focus from simply adding power to a more flexible integration of that generation into the grid.

climate-energy-f18b690d71.headline: ‘Sinking’ African megacities will expose seven million people to flooding by 2050
climate-energy-f18b690d71.fulltext:
‘Sinking’ African megacities will expose seven million people to flooding by 2050
Sinking land and rising seas could expose more than seven million people living in Africa’s coastal “megacities” to flooding by the middle of the century, according to new research.
The analysis, published in Science Advances, combines satellite data with projections of sea level rise to assess the risk of flooding in 20 of Africa’s most populous coastal cities.
The study finds that, under a moderate warming scenario, an “extreme sea level event” – when sea levels are unusually high due to short-term changes in weather and ocean conditions – could expose a million buildings and $180bn of assets to flooding.
Lagos, the capital of Nigeria, and Alexandria in Egypt are the most vulnerable cities in the analysis.
In these two cities alone, five million people and $150bn in assets could be exposed to flooding and the cities by mid-century.
Human activity, such as pumping groundwater or drilling for fossil fuels, can cause the ground to sink, in a process called “subsidence”.
Seismic or volcanic activity can also drive changes in the height of the land, causing it to either rise or fall. This “vertical land movement” can either alleviate or exacerbate the effects of sea level rise.
The researchers combined more than 4,000 satellite images of Africa’s coastline to determine how quickly different regions are rising or sinking.
They identified Lagos and Alexandria as “subsidence hotspots”, finding that the two cities are sinking at rates of 5.2mm and 6.3mm per year, respectively.
This is “comparable to rates reported for south-east Asian megacities such as Jakarta, Manila and Ho Chi Minh City”, which have recorded “some of the highest subsidence rates yet observed”, according to the study.
The authors combined these estimates with sea level rise projections from the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s sixth assessment report under three different emissions scenarios, to assess the regional sea level rise across the African coastline.
They used 2020 population data, building footprints and GDP per capita to estimate how much of each city would be exposed to these flooding events over the 21st century, if the city itself stays the same.
While Lagos and Alexandria are the most vulnerable cities, the research finds that Djibouti City in Djibouti, Mogadishu in Somalia and Tripoli in Libya will face “minimal economic exposure due to their smaller populations and infrastructure bases”.
Lead author Oluwaseyi Dasho, a PhD student at Virginia Tech, tells Carbon Brief that the analysis holds population and city data constant at 2020 levels, so that the authors can isolate the effects of sea level rise and vertical land movement on changing flood exposure.
He notes that if people move away from “threatened areas” over the coming decades, then estimates could be too high. However, if “continued urban growth” causes city populations to increase, the estimates could be too low.
Africa is the world’s fastest-urbanising region, with cities growing at an average rate of 3.5% every year. By 2050, Africa’s urban population is expected to double from 7m to 1.4bn.
He also notes that “the flood model assumes no coastal defenses, so the estimates are a worst-case physical picture”.
Subsidence in African coastal cities has not been consistently monitored in the past, largely due to a lack of local data, the study explains.
The authors say their method of using satellites to assess subsidence and uplift could be used in other “data-scarce coastal regions across the global south”.

India added 4.7GW of new rooftop solar PV capacity in Q3 2026, more than double the figure added in the same period last year, according to figures from research firm Mercom India.
Q3 2026 was the top quarter on record for rooftop solar installations in India, Mercom data shows, and in the first nine months of 2026 the country added 11.2GW of rooftop solar capacity, a 127.5% increase on the same period 2025.
In Q3, rooftop solar accounted for around 42% of India’s total solar capacity additions – a notable proportion for a country where utility-scale solar has long been the dominant market.
Over the course of 2026, residential installations have been the dominant driver of rooftop additions, largely due to the government’s PM Surya Ghar subsidy scheme for residential solar. In Q3, 95.2% of rooftop additions were on residential properties, and over the first nine months of the year, India has added around 9.9GW of residential capacity, with just over 1GW of commercial, industrial and governmental installations combined.
Mercom said that almost 5.95 million households had installed rooftop solar as of September 2026, and another 3.7 million applications were pending, representing over 10GW of potential PV installation capacity.
The states of Uttar Pradesh, Maharashtra and Gujarat led regional installations in Q3, accounting for 17%, 15% and 13%, respectively.
In Q3, rooftop systems using Chinese-made mono-PERC solar modules were markedly cheaper than Indian-made TOPCon systems that complied with the government’s domestic content requirement (DRC) measures. Chinese PERC systems went as low as INR29.7 million/MW (US$320,000/MW), while DRC TOPCon systems hit INR44.4 million/MW.
A report in May from the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis (IEEFA) said that rooftop solar installations had been a major driver of India’s expanding solar capacity since the PM Surya Ghar scheme was introduced, and it has seen 2026 become a landmark year for distributed solar across India.

global-economics-eb6eb9cf3b.headline: India Inc tightens third-party vendor checks over data breach liability ahead of DPDP Act deadline
global-economics-eb6eb9cf3b.fulltext:
NEW DELHI: Companies are tightening checks on vendors as they share more customer data with third-party service providers amid concerns over misuse and liability for breaches.
They are asking why vendors need specific data and demanding clarity on storage, access and deletion ahead of India's 13 May 2027 compliance deadline under the Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act.
Organizations now want evidence rather than attestations: where data lives, how long it is kept, who else touches it and how fast a breach is reported, said Rajat Deshpande, co-founder and chief executive of third-party service provider FinBox.
“Audit rights, deletion timelines and sub-processor disclosure are becoming standard terms rather than negotiated extras,” he said.
Major enterprises in banking, fintech and consumer services act as data fiduciaries—entities that collect personal data—while outsourcing functions such as onboarding, verification, loan collections and customer support. Third-party service providers typically process that data on their behalf across multiple touchpoints outside the company's immediate control.
Under the DPDP Act, a company cannot shift legal blame onto a vendor for a breach. Section 8 requires fiduciaries to execute proper contracts and ensure vendors maintain adequate security safeguards. If a breach occurs, the fiduciary remains primarily accountable to the Data Protection Board, which can impose penalties of up to ₹250 crore for failing to take reasonable protective steps.
“The vendor’s failure becomes the fiduciary’s problem, and the only way back to the vendor is a contractual claim under the data processing agreement with the vendor where the data fiduciary would be able to claim back-to-back monetary protection,” said Anupam Shukla, a partner at law firm Pioneer Legal.
Some companies are moving to closer technical oversight.
“Rather than relying only on contractual assurances, some are considering bringing processors within their own perimeter so that they can directly monitor the controls and security applied to their data instead of depending on periodic attestations,” said Sundareshwar Krishnamurthy, partner and India cyber leader at PwC India.
Ranking vendors
Companies are also ranking vendors by data exposure rather than contract size.
“A vendor printing employee identity cards may account for a relatively small share of the company’s overall business but could still have access to significant amounts of personal information,” said Nikhil Jhanji, principal product manager at identity verification company IDfy.
Financial institutions are increasingly focusing on vendors’ security practices, particularly around data storage, encryption standards and periodic audits.
“Critical vendors undergo periodic audits, usually once a year. We also examine their data storage practices and check whether their encryption mechanisms are being regularly upgraded,” said Kiran Pai, head of information security at credit management infrastructure company Vegapay.
Beyond contractual agreements, mechanisms are needed to verify whether vendors adhere to obligations, particularly when customer data moves across multiple systems and applications.
“A contract may require a vendor to stop processing customer data, but the institution also needs to know whether that instruction has reached the vendor’s application and whether the processing has actually stopped,” said Deepak Chand Thakur, co-founder and CEO of fintech and digital payments technology firm NPST.
Financial responsibility after a vendor-linked breach has become a flashpoint in contract talks. If a company pays a vendor ₹10 crore a year and caps liability at annual fees, the vendor may face little exposure even if a breach causes ₹100 crore in damages.
Clients want breach-related losses carved out of liability caps, while vendors resist uncapped exposure given statutory penalties of up to ₹250 crore.
“Clients want breach-related losses carved out of the cap. Vendors resist because a cap of 12 months' fees means little against penalties of ₹200-250 crore. Super-caps, specific cyber insurance requirements and fault-based allocation are where most deals settle,” said Rodney D. Ryder, founding partner at law firm Scriboard Advocates and Legal Consultants.
Shadow AI
Third-party risk predates the DPDP Act, with the Reserve Bank of India issuing outsourcing risk-management guidelines to regulated entities in 2013.
Recent incidents have kept pressure high: AU Small Finance Bank disclosed a potential data leak in October involving a third-party platform hosted and managed by Salesforce used for vehicle-loan onboarding, and cryptocurrency exchange CoinDCX reported in November that a breach at a third-party service provider exposed some customer data.
Unapproved artificial intelligence tools add another layer of exposure when employees or vendors use external models to process client records outside organizational controls.
“Companies need to understand whether vendors are using external AI tools to process client or personal data, whether appropriate safeguards are in place, and whether such data could be exposed through public or shared AI models,” said Kumar Subramaniam, chief risk officer at data analytics company Straive. “The use of unapproved third-party AI applications, often referred to as shadow AI, is becoming an important area of concern.”
Tighter scrutiny is pushing compliance costs down the supply chain, particularly for smaller technology firms, business process outsourcing units and IT service providers facing heavier security questionnaires, audits and evidence demands. Smaller vendors may need independent security audits and dedicated compliance staff to stay on enterprise lists.
“We expect procurement teams to cut vendor lists and favour certified players, which will push smaller firms toward roll-ups or acquisition by larger platforms that want their client books. Thus, smaller vendors who invest early in certification may find that compliance becomes a selling point rather than a cost,” Shukla said.

global-economics-e0c0359103.headline: Dollar Rises Toward Best Monthly Streak Since 2024 on AI Risk
global-economics-e0c0359103.fulltext:
BloombergPublished28 Nov 2026, 02:48 AM IST
(Bloomberg) -- The dollar climbed toward its longest monthly winning streak in two years as a rupture in the artificial intelligence trade and rising interest rates spur demand for safe-haven assets.
The Bloomberg Dollar Spot Index edged up on Friday and is 1.9% higher in November, putting it on track for a third straight month of gains. The greenback has strengthened against all of its Group-of-10 peers, including the Japanese yen and the Swiss franc.
A slump in technology stocks, coupled with robust economic growth and elevated inflation, propelled the dollar higher over the past three months. The US currency drew support from a flight to safety early Wednesday, when a sharp selloff briefly pushed the Nasdaq 100 into a bear market. This week, the dollar is set to rise 0.2%, extending its longest weekly winning streak since January 2025.
“It’s a pretty good dollar storm,” said Steven Englander, co-head of FX research and North America macro strategy at Standard Chartered.
Market repricing for a more hawkish Federal Reserve also supported the dollar this month, according to Sarah Ying, CIBC’s head of FX strategy.
Traders are fully pricing a 25 basis point interest rate hike next month for the Fed, and are betting on the possibility of two additional increases by the middle of next year. Policymakers have been flagging the need for more tightening, with some calling for lifting rates at successive meetings, while others are open to the possibility of raising by more than the usual quarter percentage point in December.
Some Wall Street strategists expect the dollar rally to extend into 2027, pointing to the very AI spending binge that’s making stock markets jittery as a driver of US economic growth and capital flows. The greenback has benefited from overseas investors converting local currencies to buy shares of US companies that use the tech.
“The US economy is booming and inflation is still moving away from the target,” said Win Thin, chief economist at Bank of Nassau 1982. “The Fed needs to hike rates to help cool the economy, perhaps in both December and January. That’s dollar positive.”
The dollar’s latest surge has won over short-dated options traders, but conviction further out has weakened over the past two months. The divergence suggests investors are positioning for dollar strength into early 2027 while becoming less willing to extend bullish bets much further.
The latest equities selloff has raised concerns about the longevity of the AI boom, fueling sharp swings in global markets. In such an environment, the dollar has become “the haven of choice,” according to Goldman Sachs, while MUFG believes that the prospect of higher rates is also helping the currency.
“Weakness in the US equity market is taking place at a time when there is building evidence of strengthening cyclical growth momentum in the US, which is encouraging a stronger US dollar as a safe haven play,” said Lee Hardman, senior currency analyst at MUFG.
“The strength of the US economy supports the view of investors that returns are likely to remain higher in the US even if they are currently being challenged by the recent sell-off in US assets,” he said.

global-economics-49ae24a78b.headline: No stay for Tata Trusts: HC lets Tata Sons board meet, casting vote intact
global-economics-49ae24a78b.fulltext:
Nehal ChaliawalaUpdated27 Nov 2026, 09:38 PM IST Mumbai: The Bombay High Court on Friday allowed Tata Sons to hold its board meeting on Monday, rejecting a plea by two Tata trusts to bar the company from using a tie-breaker vote. Any decisions taken at the meeting will remain subject to the outcome of the case, which will next be heard on 21 January. “Let the meeting go on,” Justice Abhay Ahuja said after more than three hours of arguments from nine senior lawyers, including Harish Salve, Abhishek Manu Singhvi and Mukul Rohatgi. The court declined interim relief to Sir Dorabji Tata Trust (SDTT) and RD Tata Trust (RDTT), which together own 30.17% of Tata Sons. The trusts fear a repeat of what happened on 17 September. At that board meeting, Tata Trusts nominee Noel Tata voted against giving chairman N Chandrasekaran a fresh term, while fellow nominee Venu Srinivasan voted for it. Independent director Harish Manwani, who chaired the discussion, then used his deciding vote to approve the resolution, prompting objections from Noel. About 200 people filled the courtroom on Friday to witness one of the most closely watched corporate battles in recent memory: Tata Trusts, which owns about two-thirds of Tata Sons, suing the board of the very company it controls. The immediate effect of Friday’s order is to allow Tata Sons to proceed with its planned steps towards becoming a public company within six months, despite opposition from Tata Trusts chairman Noel Tata. However, any board decision on Monday, including a move to call an extraordinary general meeting (EGM), will remain subject to the court’s final order, an executive aware of the matter said. “There is a possibility that the manner of voting at the earlier board meeting may be replicated, which would affect Tata Trusts’ interests. However, the fact that the decisions will be subject to the Bombay High Court’s order would offer some relief,” said Gaurav Pingle, a partner at Pune-based corporate law firm Forefront Legal Consulting LLP. Friday’s ruling is a win for Tata Sons, but a conditional one, according to an executive privy to the developments. Any resolution passed by the board, including steps towards a public listing, could be set aside if the Trusts succeed in the case in January, the executive said. Tata Sons’ agenda for Monday includes a proposal to call an EGM, following the RBI’s letters dated 11 September and 16 November. At the meeting, the company wants to put two resolutions before shareholders: the reappointment of Chandrasekaran for a third five-year term and the steps required to take Tata Sons public. The Trusts contend that the tie-breaking vote violated Article 121 of Tata Sons’ articles of association, which they say requires a majority of their nominee directors to vote in favour of a resolution. “A majority of two is two and not one,” Tata Trusts had said in September. Their counsel cautioned on Friday that the board could use the same approach again, and that any decision taken in this manner “could not easily be reversed”. “This is a foot in the door for the Trusts,” said a second executive privy to the developments. “Simply because all decisions, including the reappointment of chairman Chandrasekaran on 17 September using the casting vote, are now conditional on the outcome of this case.” Tata Trusts’ counsel Abhishek Manu Singhvi argued that the articles of association give a majority of the Trusts’ nominee directors the right to an affirmative vote before a matter proceeds to a subsequent board vote. At the 17 September meeting, when the two nominees—Noel Tata and Venu Srinivasan—failed to reach a consensus, a majority was not achieved. As a result, the resolution to reappoint Chandrasekaran for another term did not receive the required affirmative vote, he argued. Manwani, therefore, could not cast a deciding vote when the nominee directors had not reached a majority, Singhvi said. The resolution had failed once the affirmative vote was absent, he argued. Tata Sons’ counsel Harish Salve said the situation had been created by the Trusts themselves. They had nominated two directors, leading to a deadlock between them, he argued. Tata Sons’ rules allow for a board of between five and 15 members, and the Trusts had never suggested appointing more nominees, which could have given them a larger representation on the board, Salve said. “Who created this problem? The trustees did. They cannot now convert Article 121 from saying majority to unanimity,” Salve said. He added that the situation amounted to Tata Sons being held hostage by the Trusts’ nominee directors, whose inability to agree was paralysing the board’s proceedings. He accused Noel Tata of creating a situation in which only decisions he approved could be passed. Salve then listed the matters the Tata Sons board would discuss on Monday and argued that none was urgent enough to warrant postponing the meeting. On the proposed listing of Tata Sons to comply with the RBI’s directives, another point of disagreement between the Trusts and the company, Salve said the matter would come up for a shareholder vote in any case. The Trusts could use their majority to vote against it, he argued. Pausing the 30 November meeting, meanwhile, would force the company to act on Noel Tata’s terms. Senior advocate Janak Dwarkadas, representing Noel Tata, said the matter was not about Noel personally. Any nominee trustee, including Venu Srinivasan, could vote against a resolution; if the required affirmative vote was not secured, the resolution could be defeated, he argued. “We are not concerned with what they decide in the meeting,” Singhvi said. “The ground I am raising for interim [relief] is subject-neutral. It depends on an article which cuts across any subject. The article says anything which requires voting,” he said. Tata Sons and Tata Trusts did not immediately respond to Mint’s emails seeking comment. Nehal Chaliawala Nehal chronicles India’s top conglomerates for Mint. From navigating the complexities of big-bang mergers and large-scale fundraises to decoding high-profile recruitments and seemingly inexplicable corporate pivots, Nehal focuses on unpacking the long-term strategies of the country’s most influential business houses. He aims to provide readers with a clear-eyed view of how these corporate titans shape the broader Indian economy.

His professional journey began at The Economic Times in 2018, where he spent over five years before joining Mint in 2023. Over his career, he has tracked diverse sectors like automobiles, metals, cement, power, infrastructure, and renewable energy. He also keeps a close watch on the intricacies of corporate finance and corporate governance. This wide-ranging sectoral experience allows him to better understand India’s large conglomerates that sit at the confluence of these vital industries.
